item.title: September and the Second Shift
item.description:
Parenting

September and the Second Shift

Back-to-school preparation exposes the unequal mental load mothers still carry.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • School and workplace schedules often do not accommodate one another.
  • Back-to-school preparation involves cognitive and emotional work that extends far beyond buying supplies.
  • Mothers often remain responsible for this cognitive and emotional labor.

It seems like only yesterday that my friend was taking her children to band camp, describing both her excitement and apprehension as she dropped off her youngest. Now, she is posting his “first day” school photos to Instagram. It seems like parents hardly get a break between summer activities and the beginning of school; the emotional and mental labor just increasingly ramps up.

Back-to-school preparation is way more than what appears to be a collection of errands on a to-do list. It seems to represent a form of parental investment directed toward a deeper psychological goal: helping your child enter a social environment prepared to learn, perform, connect, and belong.

In some ways, back-to-school season has become the ultimate display of that investment. It’s now practically a holiday of its own. Walk into Target and you will find elaborate displays of notebooks, lunchboxes, backpacks, and dorm décor rivaling those put out for Halloween or Christmas. The range of choices suggests that there is a right backpack, lunchbox, or first-day outfit—and, by implication, wrong ones. Online, the ritual becomes even more visible. Social media fills with first-day photos, dorm-room reveals, and sorority recruitment videos. Beneath the color-coordinated bedding and carefully selected outfits are concerns familiar to parents of children at almost every age: Will my child fit in? Will they succeed?

Preparing Children to Belong

From an evolutionary perspective, humans have an unusually long childhood during which children depend on adults for resources, protection, learning, and help navigating complex relationships. Parental investment includes the time, energy, attention, and resources parents devote to their children, often at a cost to other opportunities.

For humans, this investment extends far beyond physical survival. Children must make friends, manage their budding reputations, and compete for limited opportunities. Preliminary research suggests that parents are sensitive to both the competitive and social outcomes of these interactions, wanting their children not only to succeed, but also to fit in, making investment competitive. This is why the details of back-to-school preparation can feel so consequential. A forgotten permission slip can mean missing the field trip. The wrong uniform can make a child stand out when they desperately want to blend in. The supplies, routines, outfits, and early social contact become tools for helping a child enter the group feeling confident rather than out of place. However, behind every polished first-day photo is work that the image doesn’t show.

Someone scheduled the physical, completed the forms, tracked the supply list, reset the sleep schedule, and monitored the school portal. Someone checked whether last year’s shoes still fit and remembered that their child no longer eats turkey sandwiches. Someone also worried about whether the child would recognize a friendly face and walk through the doors feeling confident. That “someone” is still disproportionately likely to be a mother.

The Thinking Behind the Doing

Sociologist Allison Daminger identifies components of cognitive household labor such as anticipating needs, identifying possible solutions, making decisions, and monitoring results. In interviews with heterosexual couples, women performed more of this labor overall, and especially more of the anticipation and monitoring, even when decision-making appeared relatively equal.

Likewise, a study of 3,000 U.S. parents illustrates how gendered this responsibility remains. Across 21 tasks, mothers reported carrying 71% of the total cognitive household labor, compared with 45% reported by fathers. The gap was even wider for the 15 routine, day-to-day tasks that keep families functioning (e.g. creating meals; scheduling appointments): Mothers reported carrying 79% of this daily cognitive labor, compared with 37% reported by fathers.

When School and Work Collide

Outside of the home, work does not make this load any easier. September does not produce work-family conflict because mothers are insufficiently organized; rather, it exposes a structural mismatch between schools and workplaces. Schools frequently operate as though someone is available for orientations, early dismissals, nurse calls, extracurricular activities, and requests sent with little notice. Workplaces operate as though employees have someone else handling those demands. All of which impacts mom's career.

Research involving nearly 38,000 U.S. mothers found that, in states with more expensive childcare and shorter average school days, mothers were less likely to work full-time and more likely to work part-time. These findings suggest that the mismatch between work and school schedules can shape mothers’ employment even after their children enter school.

This collision may be especially consequential in mid-career, when professionals are expected to demonstrate availability, assume leadership responsibilities, and accept demanding assignments, which, when in conflict, can lead to emotional exhaustion and exit consideration. None of a mother’s back-to-school labor appears on her work calendar, but it draws from the same finite supply of time, attention, and emotional energy required for professional performance.

Sharing Ownership, Not Just Errands

Meaningful relief requires transferring ownership rather than assigning isolated chores. This means sharing responsibility for school communication, anticipating deadlines, completing forms, resolving conflicts, and following up, and not waiting to be told what to do.

Employers should also recognize that the beginning of the school year is a predictable period of increased caregiving demand. Temporary scheduling flexibility, fewer unnecessary early-morning meetings, and caregiver leave can protect employees’ attention without treating caregiving as evidence of insufficient commitment. These options must be equally available, and socially acceptable, for fathers. If mothers remain the default contact for every nurse’s call, missing permission slip, and forgotten lunch, their workdays will remain fragmented while fathers’ employment remains comparatively protected.

The smiling first-day photograph does capture a child’s new chapter, but what it rarely showcases is the second shift that made that beginning possible, or the mother standing behind the camera, already thinking about what needs to happen tomorrow.

item.title: When Love Hurts—and How the Power of Attachment Explains It
item.description:
Relationships

When Love Hurts—and How the Power of Attachment Explains It

Why our brains make romance exhilarating and loss so painful.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Romantic love often relies on fantasy and expectation.
  • We frequently project our hopes, dreams, and personal happiness onto another person.
  • Love itself may not be what causes our pain; rather, it is our deep emotional attachment.

Love itself may not be what causes our pain; rather, it is our deep emotional attachment. When relationships break down, loved ones pass away, or family conflicts lead to estrangement, the core source of our distress is often the collapse of our expectations.

We frequently project our hopes, dreams, and personal happiness onto another person, making our well-being contingent on their actions. These attachments raise our expectations, leading us to demand reciprocal love and believe that others ought to treat us exactly as we treat them. When those prospects aren't met, the resulting grief and heartbreak feel like love's sting—when in reality, it is the friction of broken attachment.

Romantic love often relies on fantasy and projection—attaching to an idealized image of who a partner could be or what they represent. “We do not fall in love with a person, but with our own reflection of them,” wrote Erich Fromm from The Art of Loving.

However, true attachment requires seeing and accepting a partner's actual, grounded self. When romantic hopes demand perfection, the real person is eclipsed, preventing genuine emotional attunement and mutual regulation.

Love as Practice vs. the Trap of Idealization

As author bell hooks highlights in her book, All About Love, love is far more than a mere feeling—it is an active practice. True love is a combination of care, commitment, knowledge, responsibility, respect, and trust. It is a selfless way of being, centered on giving, presence, and supporting another person's growth without expecting something in return.

In contrast, "falling in love" often traps us in unrealistic expectations and infatuation. When we are consumed by romantic passion, we risk becoming attached to the idealization and focused primarily on how the other person makes us feel. This attachment to perfection creates high hopes that inevitably lead to pain, even in long-lasting partnerships.

When romantic desire clouds our sight, we confuse what we get from someone with how we love them. Moving forward, consider this core question: Do you love someone because you need them to fill a void in your life, or because you genuinely want to support their growth, evolution, and success? Deep love exists in the latter—free from anticipation and rooted entirely in selfless action. Love has nothing to do with possessiveness.

Human attachment is biologically designed to ensure survival, procreation, and the care of future generations. Because these evolutionary bonds are deeply wired and emotionally intense, their disruption feels catastrophic. When a bond breaks, we often claim that "love stinks"—but love itself isn't to blame.

The Neurobiology of Attachment

Romantic love introduces intense psychological and neurochemical dynamics that can sometimes overwhelm us. Here are a few of them:

Neurochemical Hijacking: Early romantic love operates on brain chemicals like dopamine, adrenaline, and phenylethylamine (PEA), which trigger intense craving, idealization, and obsessive focus. In contrast, secure attachment relies on oxytocin, endorphins, and predictable, calm co-regulation. The dramatic highs and lows of romantic passion can undermine the steady consistency needed to establish a grounded attachment base.

Triggering Attachment Insecurity: Romantic intimacy requires deep vulnerability, often activating latent attachment wounds—such as anxious or avoidant styles—that typically lie dormant in casual or platonic relationships.

Hyper-Activation of the Amygdala: Because romantic partners hold immense emotional weight, minor mis-attunements or fears of rejection trigger the brain's primitive threat response. This panic leads either to hyper-activating behaviors like clinging and criticism or deactivating responses like stonewalling and withdrawal, both of which erode closeness.

The Fear of Loss: As romantic attachment deepens, the perceived stakes rise significantly, amplifying the fear of betrayal, abandonment, and grief.

Beyond Fantasy: Building Lasting Intimacy

Romantic passion serves merely as an overture—a thrilling, high-energy introduction to connection—rather than the foundation of a life together. When infatuation completely overpowers true attachment, or when unhealed emotional wounds prevent authentic vulnerability, the relationship inevitably fractures. No connection can survive indefinitely on the high-wire of idealization, where perfection is demanded and projection eclipses reality.

True intimacy cannot survive in the rarefied air of romanticism; it takes root only when two people intentionally step down from the peaks of starry-eyed naiveté and ground themselves in the quiet, unvarnished reality of everyday life. This transition is not a surrender, but an evolution. It asks us to dismantle impossible, high-stakes hopes and replace them with the patient, continuous work of mutual attunement—the daily discipline of recognizing, accepting, and tenderly honoring one another as flawed human beings. By choosing presence over perfection, we slowly convert the volatile spark of initial longing into a sanctuary of emotional safety. In the end, lasting connection isn't something we fall into—it is a secure home we construct together. As the late clinical psychologist Dr. Sue Johnson observed, "We are built to need others, and the person we love is our primary anchor in the world."

item.title: Beware of the 'Dread Game' in Dating and Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

Beware of the 'Dread Game' in Dating and Relationships

The "dread game" can be a hard-to-detect form of manipulation.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • The "dread game" is when a person stokes fear that he or she might leave you in order to control you.
  • Your romantic partner might tell you about his or her other dating options or even threaten to leave.
  • "Dread game" tactics can be part of a deliberate manipulative strategy or an unintentional reflex response.
Source: Andrii Yalanskyi/Shutterstock

Well, here's a dreadful approach to dating and relationships. It's being called the "dread game" because it's when a person stokes fear in you—the fear that he or she might leave you—in order to keep you in line. Yikes.

The 'Dread Game' Is About Maintaining Fear and Worry

It's basically a twisted version of that 1995 Shania Twain song, "(If You're Not in It for Love) I'm Outta Here!" The twist here is that when a romantic partner does the "dread game," it's not for love but rather for control over you. That person wants you to believe that you are as replaceable as a pair of underwear that he or she could drop on the bathroom floor at any moment.

There are different ways that people can keep you in a state of such dread. These range from comparing you unfavorably with their exes to mentioning how others desire them so much to threatening to leave unless you do what they want you to do.

The whole "dread" thing can really rear its ugly head when the two of you disagree on something. Instead of talking through things in a mature, constructive manner, your partner may say something like "Maybe we aren't a good match," "This is how my last relationship ended," "This makes me really rethink everything about our relationship," or some other dramatic statement. This essentially flashes a red light that says, "Stop, or else I'm leaving you."

This is a shift move, so to speak, to try to flip you from arguing to reassuring your partner. This may even make you forget about the disagreement altogether. You may be particularly susceptible to such a game if you've got a fear of abandonment or being single, an anxious attachment style, or a belief that you are just not worthy of such a partner.

Once it's clear that this "red light" works on you, expect it to be flashed again and again. Your partner can always use the "I might leave you" threat to control anything that you do. This could leave you in a perpetual state of hypervigilance and worry.

The 'Dread Game' Can Be Hard to Spot

Before using such a red light on you, your partner may have to give you a bunch of green lights to get you hooked on him or her. So, the "dread game" can be preceded by a hot-and-heavy phase where your body rather than your mind begin advising you. It can also be set up by a love-bombing phase where your partner drops heavy compliments and statements like "we were meant to be with each other" on you.

All of this initial green-light stuff can camouflage the subsequent red-flag entry into the "dread game" phase of your relationship. When you start hitting red lights, you may blame yourself and focus on finding those green lights again. Your partner then can alternate green and red lights to achieve Squid Game-like control over you.

The 'Dread Game' Can Be Planned or a Reaction

While both men and women can play this "dread game," it's recently gotten attention since members of the so-called "manosphere" have been advancing it as a way to deal with women, who, in their words "don't know their place." Such manospherers claim to have taken the "red pill," revealing their so-called truth: that you either dominate or are dominated in relationships with no in-between possibilities.

Such black-and-white thinking isn't necessarily restricted to the manosphere, as plenty of men and women across different organizations, institutions, and industries think in the same zero-sum way about their professional relationships and may let such thinking spill over to personal relationships as well. All of this can stem from insecurity. Deep down, they may believe that they alone are not good enough to get what they want—whether it's advancing at work, keeping someone attracted to them, or handling a disagreement—and thus must resort to manipulation.

So, yes, any "dread game"-like tactics can certainly be part of an overall deliberate and calculated strategy. They alternatively can be unintentional learned reflexes brought on by stress, confusion, the inability to handle conflicts constructively, and ironically dread. So it's important to determine whether you are dealing with a one-time or simple misunderstanding thing versus a continuing involuntary reaction thing versus a true "dread game" thing. The number of times such red light events happen is key as once can be an accident, twice a coincidence, but three times is a trend.

How to Respond to the ‘Dread Game’

Now, if it's a true "dread game thing," you may want a relationship where one partner is dominant over the other. You may be fine with a relationship based on fear and dread. You may even get all hot and bothered by the prospect of Freddie Krueger from The Nightmare series or Annie Wilkes from the 1990 movie Misery being your partner. Everyone's is different, and you should find whomever best fits you romantically.

Assuming, though, that you do want a relationship based on mutual trust with an equal partner and stuff like that, then it's better to recognize as soon as possible when the "dread game" is being played or the red light tactics have at least become a trend. Then, don't just "dread" ahead. Make it clear that you don't tolerate such behaviors. If your partner isn't willing to change, then you can simply leave the relationship—not threaten to leave but actually leave.

Be careful, though, as your partner might in turn switch into save-the-relationship mode. This can include temporary promises to change. Taking him or her back and then doing this cycle over and over again can be kind of playing the "dread game" yourself. Therefore, put a clear limit on anything that you do.

If you truly believe your partner means well and could change, one option is to get a professional like a therapist involved. The goal would be to help your partner realize how having control is not necessary in a relationship and how to deal with differences in ways that strengthen the relationship. Don't take this option lightly, though, because such change isn't easy.

Beware of wasting too much time on someone who's never going to be a good fit for you. And don't let those who play the "dread game" make you dread the thought of dating anyone. While there may be lots of red lights out there, stay open to finding the true green lights for you.

item.title: The 5 Things That Can Happen After You Fall in Love
item.description:
Relationships

The 5 Things That Can Happen After You Fall in Love

What happens when the butterflies fade, and what your relationship becomes next.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Long-term relationships can become more satisfying when passionate love develops into deeper intimacy.
  • Boredom may call for novelty and new experiences, whereas unresolved hurt may require repair.
  • Moments of feeling misunderstood can create emotional distance long before a relationship officially ends.
Source: Ronny Overhate/Pixabay

I was sipping my coffee at the coffee shop, thinking about my next research collaboration, enjoying the greenery around me as butterflies flew by.

It was an early Saturday morning, and right in front of me, a couple was dancing in the parking lot without any music.

They were kissing, hugging, smiling. Then he walked her toward her car, they kissed again, and drove away in separate cars.

Maybe they had been married for 30 years. Maybe they were on their first date. Who knows? But watching them made me think about the butterfly phase—that crazy phase when you first fall in love. You are just flying. The trees are greener. Even when something bad happens, it doesn't feel bad because somewhere in your mind you have this feeling: I have them.

You talk for hours and still have more to say. You stay up all night talking, watch the sun come up, drive home, sleep for two hours, and wake up already missing each other. You send romantic messages. You don't care if they see you sick. You can do whatever you want in front of them and they still love you. And you realize that you just want their presence.

No wonder it feels like flying. You are discovering another person, a new world, and a new version of yourself inside that world. This is what I mean by “We fall.” But falling in love is only the beginning.

What happens after the butterflies?

I think there are five places a relationship can find itself, or maybe five possible directions.

1. We Fall. You already know this part: The butterflies. The excitement. The feeling that you have finally found your person. But nothing stays new forever. And eventually...

2. We Adapt. Our brains adapt to things that once felt extraordinary. The kisses don't give you the same butterflies anymore. The first months of excitement become years of familiarity. And maybe that is not a bad thing. We cannot live at the emotional intensity of a new relationship forever. The butterflies slow down.

Think about it this way: The butterflies can disappear without the love disappearing. After the passion fades, the relationship can go in different directions. And I want you to pay attention to the next part.

3. We Grow or We Shrink. What replaces the butterfly phase? In one possibility, the intensity becomes less and something deeper takes its place. You still feel safe with this person. You still want to know what they are thinking. You still want to show them something interesting you saw. The love is not that loud, but it is there. It has moved from: I can't live without you to I want to live this life with you. This is where passionate love can grow into a more companionate kind of love. The intimacy can be more deeper.

But there is another possibility: The butterflies disappear, and instead of deeper love, there is just routine. Work, kids, etc. Why does the relationship feel boring now? Many couples try to bring the butterflies back. They go to the restaurant where they had they first date. They to recreate the first kiss. But it doesn't work.

And they think: Is this it?

Maybe it is wrong when we try to recreate the feeling instead of creating a new reason to feel something. What if you don't need to recreate your first date? What if you need to discover each other again? We are multifaceted people, always changing, with new sides waiting to be explored. Maybe you miss the feeling of discovering something new together. So try something neither of you has done before. Go somewhere you've never been. Do something ridiculous. Discover something that makes you look at each other and think, I didn't know this side of you existed. Maybe you need a new version of each other to meet.

But sometimes, there might be another reason or a problem.

What if you are deeply hurt?

4. We Disconnect. Sometimes the butterflies disappear because too much pain has accumulated: A moment when you needed them and they weren't there. A hurt you never talked about. So you forgive. You move on—or at least you tell yourself you did. Eventually, you stop talking about it. Because what is the point? You already had this conversation. They already know. So you live around the pain instead of dealing with it. And slowly, you stop sharing things.

Why? Because you no longer believe it will make a difference.

Boredom and hurt are not the same problem. Hurt and pain need lots of work. The question is, do you want to do the work? Maybe instead you become indifferent. You stop caring. You keep living together. But emotionally, you have started living separate lives.

Sometimes love disappears through a thousand small moments when you feel less understood, less supported, less seen. And maybe the relationship ends. And then, later, strange things might happen.

5. We Return to Ourselves. The rainbow world comes back. You walk outside and suddenly the trees are green again. The flowers smell like heaven again. You want to see people. You laugh more. And you think: Wait. Were the trees always this green?

Yes, they were. The world did not suddenly become beautiful; you became available to notice it again. Maybe somewhere inside that relationship, you had stopped being fully yourself. And now you are meeting yourself again.

Maybe you had forgotten what the world felt like when your emotional state wasn't tied to another person. Is this liberation?

This brings me back to that couple in the parking lot. Maybe they lost the butterflies many years ago. Maybe they learned how to love each other after the butterflies changed. We don't know.

The goal of a long relationship, in my humble opinion, is not to feel like you are falling in love every morning for 30 years. That is probably impossible. The goal is to pay attention to what comes after them, because the butterflies are not the measure of whether love is alive.

If you are sitting in a relationship right now wondering where your butterflies went, ask this: Am I still curious about them? Am I bored or am I hurt?

And if you are no longer in that relationship, ask yourself: When the world suddenly became green again, was it because you found somebody new? Or because you finally found yourself?

Maybe the trees were never less green. Maybe you were looking at the world from a different state. So what state are you in right now?

item.title: Gossip's Brighter Side
item.description:
Relationships

Gossip's Brighter Side

Gossip: our guide through the social jungle and a handy tool for self-analysis.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Our first knee-jerk reaction frowns on gossip, but science supports its remarkable social purposes.
  • Gossip, our most on-hand "news source," keeps us up to date on pertinent local, social activity.
  • Our tongues wag quickest and most purposefully when our significant others are the "headlines."

Gossip’s muddied reputation is deeply sunk in disrepute, but once “rinsed off," its brighter side shines.

Despite its commonplace, everyday usage, the majority of us disavow gossip. We frown upon it disapprovingly, even scornfully for its customary meanings. Gossip remains putatively up to its neck in mud, mired in pejorative connotations and a social repugnancy it never sheds. But our conventional anti-gossip sentiments fly in the face of scientific findings.

Across the Spectrum

Across the social science spectrum, researchers cast gossip largely in a prosocial role because it serves vital and far-reaching functions like, human bonding, the regulation and reinforcement of social codes and mores, the deterrence of unacceptable, antisocial behavior and the navigation of interpersonal intricacies and complexities. Moreover, gossip is decidedly “our most local news source,“ keeping us informed and fueled with critical hearsay about activities occurring in our immediate social network.

By scientific reckoning, the upside of gossip far outweighs its downside, once cleansed of its ill-repute.

A Conversational Mainstay

Defined colloquially, gossip is talk about those not present. Subtract up to 80% of the content of our day-to-day conversations and the remaining 20% is gossip-free, according to research. Statistically, gossip sucks up most of the conversational oxygen by promoting an active exchange of compelling, much-needed social information, whose purpose is to actively surveil our social surroundings like a lighthouse illuminating a shoreline, especially a rocky one.

Defying its blemished reputation, studies find only 15% of our tongue-wagging about our fellow human beings is perpetrated with an intent to inflict disrepute or harm. Expectedly, our tongues wag their quickest, most deliberately, and with the greatest purpose when the subject matter is family, friends and co-workers—this is where interpersonal politics count the most but can bite the hardest.

Happily, the bulk of our gossip is neutral, devoid of barbs and thus innocuous. Moreover, the most “local news“ we get pertains to the interpersonal comings and goings occurring within our relatively tight-knit social circles. Gossip is our personally relevant and consequential news source. It confirms, disconfirms, or expands on information we collect on our own, which is often too narrow in scope.

Gossip’s Roots in Antiquity

Gossip‘s taproots stretch back to civilization’s dawning. Egyptian hieroglyphics depict “gossip“ carved on limestone flakes and broken pottery fragments preserving stories of love affairs among Egypt’s elite ruling class. Clearly, gossip is an ancient, time-tested but still very here-and-now “technology“ for steering us through the fulfilling but often rugged, zig-zag terrain of our uneven social world.

The Hardest Reality

Conversely, navigating physical reality has become increasingly easier because of non-stop advances in an expanding array of modern technologies that move us ever-more efficiently and prosperously through our physical environment. Yet for many of us, the hardest reality we navigate is social reality and, paradoxically, gossip is the “universal rudder“ that helps steer our course through the diverse, capricious and intricate world of others.

Here’s a common example: A co-worker advises a newly hired employee about their mutual boss, who’s an irascible, stickler for office policy. This small act of thoughtfulness unleashes a few of gossip‘s positive features: The new employee bonds with her mentor co-worker; she’s now more prepared in her new workplace because she’s equipped with information that will enable her to adjust to her new boss.

“Gossiphiles“ vs. “Gossiphobes“

When the opportunity pops up to talk about someone who's not there, as it frequently does, how do you feel? We’re often charged with powerful, savory incentives because of the valid reasons we have for actively sharing and gobbling up information that not only informs us but suggests how to effectively negotiate the sundry contours and the ups and downs of our social surroundings. Many of us become avid consumers, “gossiphiles,“ lovers of gossip. When done with non-malignant, data-gathering or data-sharing intentions, we enjoy the experience, it’s rare when we don’t and rarer still when we find it unappealing.

However, ambiguity can strong-arm our attitude on gossip. We love it when it’s done for prosocial intentions, but we can detest it if we or someone else stoops to defaming others. Further, stooping to the bottom of the gossip barrel can arouse our creeping suspicions of what others—who also monitor us—may be saying behind our backs; or "gossiphobia,“ the fear of gossip. Sober, pre-gossip contemplation should temper our talk about others, as they too may have things to say about us when we’re not around.

Professional Gossiper

I confess, I‘m a professional gossiper, albeit for the right intentions. As a practicing psychologist, other-talk is par for the course—I encourage it! People-troubles, hurts, and conflicts rank high on the “all-star list“ of stressors. Relationships, especially our closest ones, can be a fertile breeding ground for turmoil and conflict. Frequently, clients frame their unresolved conflicts in blaming, labeling and storytelling, gossip’s homely allies. But its flip side can be therapeutic.

Explicit vs. Implicit Stories

For example, a client openly accuses their partner of being "controlling." Once “public," the accusation can now be referred to as an “explicit story.“ However, the explicit story has its counterpart, an “implicit story,“ the unarticulated story the accuser “tells“ about themself without being fully aware of it. That is, for someone to play the role of controller there must be someone else playing the role of “controllee." Both roles are complementary; one can’t exist without the other, just as there are no teachers without students or doctors without patients, etc.

Embedded in the accuser’s implicit story are the accuser’s needs that are not being identified, much less managed. But unveiled, they often consist of the accuser’s needs to “play it safe" or to maintain harmony and avoid conflict or evade the risks of managing their needs assertively. It‘s often easier to gossip or tell an explicit story, holding others responsible for our needs, rather than do the harder task of managing personal needs that aren’t always easily managed.

Analyze your intentions and the content of your gossip. It can be self-revealing.

item.title: Why “Tony” Fails and What Therapists Can Learn From It
item.description:
Media

Why “Tony” Fails and What Therapists Can Learn From It

The film “Tony” is a tale of redemption without contrition.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists need to track if patients' levels of contrition are sufficient to afford them true redemption.
  • The film "Tony" portrays a character who isn't sorry for being narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless.
  • Many of us go to the cinema to see sympathetic characters become better humans.
  • "Tony" delivers a happy ending that isn't earned.

Many of us go to the cinema to witness sympathetic characters overcome external and internal obstacles and become better humans (or tragically die trying). There are archetypal heroes' journeys—and now there are fresh archetypal heroines' journeys emerging, too. These narratives inspire us to be more authentic, to the be heroes and heroines of our own lives.

A bildungsroman is a novel of formation that tracks a young protagonist through the shedding of childish illusions as they individuate and gain a mature understanding of themselves, life, and the world. Unlike a typical adventure, a bildungsroman insists that its hero pays for growth in genuine psychological currency: confusion, failure, grief, humiliation, and the process of taking accountability for one's own mistakes, transcending one's failures, and insuring that the same mistakes are never made again. Catcher in the Rye is one American version of a bildungsroman because Holden Caulfield's journey through New York is a psychological rebellion and exploration, a wandering through artifice and loss that doesn't allow him to escape unscathed. By the end, Holden arrives, through exhaustion and honesty, at a more complete and authentic understanding of himself, life, and the people he loves, which is precisely what the genre asks of its heroes and heroines. But could this not also be a reductionistic description of successful Lacanian psychoanalysis as well? And we could add a tinge of Tara Brach's "radical acceptance" as well?

The new film Tony, about the early life of Anthony Bourdain, opens with a quote from his best-selling autobiography: "I was—to be frank—a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive, and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking." The film ends with Tony, barely, by chance, luck, or fate, not stealing from the mentor who tried to help him transition from boyhood to manhood, the mentor whose business Tony has already torched. It's admirable to have the awareness that one is in need of a good ass-kicking, but what happens when that ass-kicking isn't accompanied by sufficient remorse and contrition, or doesn't come at all?

Compare the end of Tony with, for example, Sylvester Stallone's level of contrition during his search for redemption toward the end of his 1997 film, Copland:

Stallone's character, a New Jersey sheriff, recognizes that he messed up and wants to be a "stand-up guy." Informed that he is too late, Stallone has the equivalent of a psychoanalytic "aha" moment, a visceral realization that draws people both to therapy and to the flickers.

While Tony borrows the outer shape of a bildungsroman, it doesn't satisfy its inner requirements. It's wonderful that Bourdain realized that he was a narcissistic, selfish lout, but in the film the character of Tony is practically devoid of remorse and contrition. Whereas Holden Caulfield earns whatever understanding he reaches through pages of confusion and honest self-accounting, Tony casually and narrowly avoids a life of crime. There is no scene in which he seeks out the mentor he has wronged and begs for forgiveness.

Don't get me started on male brooding in films as a poor man's emotional intelligence. I similarly loathed Jeremy Allen's brooding in Springsteen: Deliver Me from Nowhere; similarly, Dominic Sessa's excessive pouting while portraying Bourdain is simply poor filmmaking. "Show, don't tell," is the adage screenwriters are meant to adhere to. On-screen moping is a compensation for deficient screenwriting.

Thus Tony delivers a happy ending that isn't earned. Tony enters adulthood learning, mostly, that he could get away with being a lout and that the world would tolerate and maybe even reward his narcissism—which is the opposite of what a true coming-of-age story necessitates: a hero who becomes capable of guilt, who takes responsibility for the wreckage he caused, and authentically seeks redemption with sufficient contrition. Although Tony surreptitiously redeems himself at the end, he lacks sufficient remorse and thus remains for me a lout. This is what therapists often need to track in session—whether the patient's level of contrition is sufficient to afford them true redemption.

item.title: Can I Lose Weight by Eating Gelatin?
item.description:
Diet

Can I Lose Weight by Eating Gelatin?

Does the “gelatin trick” really fool the stomach into feeling full?

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • The claim is that gelatin taken before eating forms a gel that reduces food intake leading to weight loss.
  • The gelling process never occurs in the stomach, and clinical studies show no evidence of weight loss.

As a scientist who studies the impact of nutrition on the brain and general health, I try to stay up to date on popular diets. One of my students pointed me in the direction of claims in Facebook groups and popular wellness communities online that a common diet ingredient, gelatin, can help reduce body weight. It’s called "the overnight gelatin habit." Proponents claim that it’s a simple daily ritual to calm hunger signals that doesn’t require prescriptions, food tracking, or exercise.

That's an amazing claim, but things that sound too good to be true usually are.

We are all familiar with the popular food Jell-O. The name is clever because it is a play on “gelatin,” the peptide that turns flavored water into a jelly. Today pseudoscience influencers are pushing the message that a tablespoon of gelatin, the precursor to Jell-O, if taken a half-hour before eating, will leave no room for other foods in the stomach and therefore lead to weight loss.

Gelatin can turn water into a thickened gel. That molecular magic has been known since antiquity when farmers discovered that boiling animal skins, bones or tendons produces a broth that sets into a solid jelly on cooling. We now understand the chemistry of this phenomenon. Collagen is a protein extracted by hot water from animal tissues. When it is sufficiently heated, the large collagen molecules break down into smaller peptides called gelatin. The small gelatin peptides move freely in solution; as the solution cools, they form weak bonds with each other, trapping water molecules in the process—resulting, when combined with flavorings, in a tasty gel. [Pearle Bixby Wait, in 1897, a carpenter who was searching for a cough remedy and laxative tea, is credited, along with his wife, May, of inventing and naming the fruit-flavored dessert Jell-O.]

Does the gelatin claim make sense?

The claim that gelatin forms a gel that fills the stomach is bogus. To produce a gel, gelatin has to be heated and then cooled. This will not happen at 37oC, roughly the temperature of the stomach. As anyone who has ever made Jell-O knows, the water has to be heated to near boiling to dissolve the gelatin. Obviously, that will never happen. So, gelling in the stomach is not a legitimate claim for the supposed appetite-reducing effect of gelatin.

How did this rumor go viral?

In the case of gelatin, the concept arose from a study from Holland’s Maastricht University. It’s a well-known fact that some proteins can suppress the appetite. The researchers investigated whether the specific amino acid content is important. They compared the milk protein casein, which contains a good balance of all the amino acids that we need, to gelatin, which does not contain a complete balance of all the essential amino acids. The hypothesis was that the lack of essential amino acids would cause the body to reject an imbalanced diet and result in a suppression of hunger. [For more, click here.]

The study design was flawed. Subjects were simply asked to give a numerical estimate to the question “How hungry do you feel right now?” at various times after consuming a meal that contained at least 50 grams of gelatin or an equal amount of casein. 50 grams is considerably more than the 7-8 grams of gelatin found in 1 tablespoon, which is the amount recommended online for the “gelatin weight-loss trick” to work. The study reported that the 50-gram dose of gelatin did suppress hunger—but failed to determine whether the subjects consumed less food! This study is often referenced by online supporters of this diet; unfortunately, the study never presented evidence of reduced food intake in response to the gelatin. A later study by the same lab (Hochstenbach-Waelen et al., 2010) followed 72 overweight people who over 8 weeks consumed a gelatin-laced meal that, according to the previous study, should have reduced calorie intake at the next meal and therefore lead to weight loss. It didn’t. The study failed to show any weight loss associated with consumption of gelatin.

Gelatin’s supposed trick of causing weight loss is just an illusion.

item.title: Psychoanalysis Works—And It Doesn’t Owe You a Brain Scan
item.description:
Psychoanalysis

Psychoanalysis Works—And It Doesn’t Owe You a Brain Scan

Why therapeutic meaning can’t always be measured in neuroscience.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Psychoanalysis is both deeply familiar and uncomfortably strange.
  • While many would like to reduce analysis to its neurophysiological counterparts, I argue we should not.
  • Core psychoanalytic ideas echo universal human wisdoms about relationships and personal growth.
Source: Max Halberstadt, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Scott Stossel begins his Atlantic article entitled “What If Freud Was Right?” with the following provocation:

“To announce that you are embarking on a course of psychoanalytic training today is tantamount, in many quarters, to admitting that you plan to treat your patients using astrology or by parsing the entrails of a goat. To say that you are undergoing psychoanalysis as a patient is to reveal that you are entrusting your mental health to a witch doctor.”

As a recent graduate of a psychoanalytic training program (and therefore, as an analytic patient myself), I can attest that both of these statements are essentially true. But Stossel is not writing a criticism of psychoanalysis. Instead he is half-reviewing, half-musing on the new book by the well-known neuroscientist and psychoanalyst Mark Solms, The Only Cure: Freud and the Neuroscience of Mental Healing. While he does do his journalistic due diligence, reviewing some of the studies Solms cites and pointing out that Solms (like many academic authors of books written for the public) has cherry-picked the studies he builds his strongly-worded thesis around, the heart of the piece seems to be about his surprise over Solms’ enthusiasm for Freudian theory and practice.

Solms, argues Stossel, is making two astonishing arguments. One, that Freud was presciently accurate about many now established models of neurophysiology (the unconscious, the encoding of short-term into long-term memories, the “pleasure-principle,” and others). And the other, that of all the treatments we now have at our disposal for the treatment of mental suffering of any diagnostic sort, psychoanalytic-type treatments are what lead to cure.

Stossel’s Perspective on Psychoanalytic Theories

Stossel reads as somewhat baffled by this conclusion throughout his piece, as though he can’t quite believe he is the one writing it. Indeed, he himself says “Some people—and by some people, I might mean me—derive a certain solace from understanding their anxiety and depression as, in effect, mechanical failures, not moral ones: a snag in the temperamental wiring here, an unfortunate genetic variant there, a dysregulation of neurotransmitters not unlike the problems with insulin regulation in a diabetic’s pancreas.” I have the sense that he can’t choose which narrative feels more accurate—the biological “mechanical failure,” or the seemingly esoteric—and until recently, safely ignored, psychoanalytic ideas. Most concerningly to Stossel, perhaps, is what Solms says about medications:

“The mainstay of modern psychiatry—psychopharmacology—is for the most part a defence against facing the facts about what our patients really need. It is a way of suppressing symptoms instead of asking what they mean and fixing that.”

Stossel goes on to express his doubts about Solms’ description of psychoanalysis, which includes “dream analysis, free association, breaking down defense mechanisms, recovering buried memories, transference and countertransference, and elaborate (too elaborate, if you ask me) feats of interpretation by the analyst. To someone with my firmly materialist leanings, it all seems a bit much.”

But in the end, Solms’ less controversial statements are what seem to resonate most comfortably for Stossel—that the core of psychoanalysis is “to help our patients find better ways of meeting their emotional needs.” And that “Psychoanalysis is a cure wrought by loving your neighbor as yourself.” These are conclusions that Stossel, and perhaps the general public, can easily accept, and that, as he says, might help to humanize psychiatry once again.

Public Perception and the Challenge of Explaining Psychoanalysis

In many ways, this article gets at the heart of psychoanalysis’s problematic public issue. Some of the theories and concepts that lay at the foundation of every school of analytic thought are difficult for those unfamiliar with them to swallow. Ideas like the unconscious mind, fantasies and conflicts that run repetitive loops in the background of all our conscious actions, transferential enactments with therapists, bosses, friends, spouses, lovers, and children, projection, displacement, repression, and denial. Even without some of the more controversial and less universal analytic theories (like the Oedipal complex, penis envy, or the death instinct, for instance), these concepts are threatening to a public that has eschewed more internal or complex understandings of their minds in favor of diagnostic labels, materialistic treatments, and a comfortable relationship with therapies that address behaviors, and occasionally thoughts, but not fantasies, transferences, or unconscious conflicts.

And yet psychoanalytic ideas about our own minds and our relationships to the minds of others echo some of the most basic human wisdoms: People need meaning in their lives to find contentment; relationships are how we both develop into people and stay physically and psychologically healthy (or not), we cannot run from our traumatic pasts; grieving what we longed for and didn’t get as children is how we ultimately move forward into maturity, and so many others. This wisdom has accumulated through the analytic community over the 150 years of psychoanalytic treatment, and echoes the teachings of Buddhist, Judeo-Christian, and Stoic philosophies, among others. To embark on a psychoanalytic journey is less medicine and more a spiritual and philosophical journey with another person into the depths of one’s own self and soul. But how to explain the journey to a public looking for a pill?

The Dilemma: Explaining Psychoanalysis in a Materialistic Culture

Here is the dilemma: psychoanalysis is both uncanny and deeply familiar, resonant and off-putting in equal measure. And the field of psychoanalysis struggles in this cultural zeitgeist to find a way to explain itself without jettisoning some of its more controversial ideas.

Solms is trying to bridge the divide with “neuropsychoanalysis,” tying the more ephemeral nature of psychoanalysis to the material world of neurons, synapses, white matter, and “predictive processing.” This reminds me of the cringe-inducing excitement of the psychoanalytic world when mirror neurons began to make headlines as a neurological explanation for therapeutic effectiveness, headlines that faded as mirror neuron findings failed to replicate. I am not against neuroscience or neurophysiological corollaries to analytic theory or practice. But I also don’t think that the field owes the public this sort of materialistic explanation. What we truly owe this cultural moment is a doubling down on the value of the ephemeral, the uncanny, the transformational mystery that is psychoanalysis. I have learned this lesson in my soul, gut, heart, and mind from both sides of the couch: what is most meaningful in life cannot be seen on an MRI, or contained in a pill.

item.title: Ageism and Retirement
item.description:
Aging

Ageism and Retirement

Nobody prepares us for ageism, though it impacts the quality of our retirement.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • During retirement, people often encounter ageism in social, medical, mental health, and workplace settings.
  • Ageism can lead to shorter lifespans, poorer physical and mental health, and cognitive decline.
  • Ageism can be overt disdain and contempt of older adults or it can be disguised as compassionate patronizing.

I recently overheard a conversation occurring amongst an assemblage of 30-year-olds. One woman was sheepishly describing her attraction to actor George Clooney when she was cut short by the vehement response of a peer.

“How can you find him attractive? He’s got to be at least 60. He’s old.”

As of the writing of this post, Mr. Clooney is actually 65 years old. I am five years younger, so this woman’s comment still stung me.

Welcome, fellow adults of my age bracket (and older), to a time of unwelcome and unfortunately inevitable ageist experiences. Nobody prepares us for them. Not even the most comprehensive retirement planning programs—those that address financial matters, the challenges of unstructured time, changing marital dynamics, loss of workplace relationships, and post-employment purpose and meaning—consider how ageism will impact our retirement years.

And ageism most certainly impacts the quality of our retirement.

The Two Types of Ageism

Research findings are quite frightening, so don’t dismiss, minimize, or trivialize the impact of ageism. Consider the World Health Organization’s Global Report on Ageism (2021), which states, “[A]geism is prevalent, ubiquitous and insidious… Ageism has serious and far-reaching consequences for people’s health, well-being and human rights and costs society billions of dollars” (p. IX).

Let’s back up a little bit and consider the history of ageism. Robert Butler first introduced the concept of ageism in 1969 and described it as "prejudice by one age group toward other age groups." Fifty years of research has been conducted since this seminal definition was introduced, and we now have a much more comprehensive understanding of ageism. Consider the 2009 definition by Iversen, Larsen, & Solem, who describe it as “negative or positive stereotypes, prejudice and/or discrimination against (or to the advantage of) elderly people on the basis of their chronological age or on the basis of a perception of them as being 'old or 'elderly'. Ageism can be implicit or explicit and can be expressed on a micro-, meso- or macro-level." Wow! What a difference.

We are going to confront two forms of ageism in our retirement years (Butler, 1980). First, we will encounter benign ageism, which is a perception of older adults as frail, dependent, and helpless. This form of ageism can lead to compassionate but also patronizing treatment; it elicits feelings of pity toward older people and leads to protective paternalism.

A recent example is a 78-year-old grandmother who was not informed that her adult grandchild had divorced; the family thought it would be too much for her. When she belatedly learned the truth, she was furious. Deleting her copious expletives, her response was along the lines of "How dare you treat me like a child!" Benign ageism is well-intentioned and infantilizing.

The second form is malignant ageism, which is a perception of older folks as a societal burden. Consider some of the descriptors of older adults all too frequently encountered: unproductive, technologically illiterate, sedentary, lonely, unattractive, unhappy, unskilled, and inactive.

Two recent examples of malignant ageism will suffice. First, the character of the grandmother in the 2025 film Song Sung Blue is introduced to us as a stereotypical crotchety burden whose family is literally waiting for a nursing home placement as soon as one becomes available.

A second and far more serious example is the frequently held belief that older workers hinder younger colleagues' career advancement, particularly promotion. Many older workers have heard outright or been the recipient of a suggestion that they step aside and make room for the next generations in the workplace. Our presence is a burden to them.

How Ageism Hurts Us

Decades of research from a multitude of fields concludes ageism hurts us physically and psychologically. Consider this statement by the American Psychological Association: “[I]f we have the good fortune to live a long life, inaccurate stereotypes about aging will harm all of us” (Weir, 2023). Supporting this conclusion, the aforementioned WHO report determined, “[A]geism is associated with a shorter lifespan, poorer physical and mental health, slower recovery from disability and cognitive decline."

What leads to these pernicious effects? Let's start with the impact of aging stereotypes on medical providers' treatment decisions. Providers misdiagnose, under-treat, or dismiss health concerns when working with older folks in addition to using “elderspeak,” including limiting vocabulary, dumbing down explanations, or speaking to family members rather than to the patients themselves, assuming they are unable to participate in decisions about their care.

In their review of the research, Swift et al. (2017) determined perceptions of aging affected physicians’ decisions, leading them to be less likely to correctly diagnose a disorder as well as provide proper treatment to older patients.

The pernicious effects of ageism don’t just happen in healthcare settings, so let’s move to the workplace. More and more baby boomers are remaining at their jobs after reaching retirement age either due to financial need or enjoyment and satisfaction with employment, a trend predicted to continue with Gen Xers. One meta-analysis explored the effect of ageism on older workers and determined it influences the process of hiring older workers, their career advancement, access to training, and performance appraisals (Bal et al. 2011).

To conclude, during our retirement years we will encounter ageism in social, medical, mental health, and workplace settings. According to Palmore (2015), “Ageism is so much a part of our culture that most people are not even aware of it. It is like the air we breathe. Most people become aware of it only when they grow old enough to suffer some discrimination...”

A Plan for Navigating Ageism

We have not been taught to prepare for ageism, an experience that can shorten our lives and lead to mental health manifestations.

Most of the research on changing ageism addresses societal change; this includes “big picture” projects to eradicate ageism, which we should wholeheartedly support. But at the individual level, suggestions are sparse. Here are five recommendations to begin today:

  • Acknowledge the reality of ageism. Everybody will experience it as we age.
  • Recognize that ageism is harmful; five decades of research support this troubling conclusion.
  • Call ageist treatment out when encountered.
  • Ask your medical and/or mental health provider about their training for working with older adults and comfort with the demographic. Better yet, ask them to read this blog posting.
  • Interact in mixed-age groups (called “intergeneration contact” in the psychology literature). These groups typically involve bringing older and younger people together to work cooperatively on tasks encouraging cross-generational bonding and understanding.

item.title: Trading Summer for Structure
item.description:
Stress

Trading Summer for Structure

Why the return to routine requires work.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • There is an emotional tax transitioning from the fluid flexibility of summer to the strict structure of fall.
  • Back-to-school success takes students, parents, teachers, coaches, guardians, and even non-parent colleagues.
  • Routines help lower workload, stress, and anxiety by minimizing the daily decisions the brain needs to make.

As the golden days of summer shorten, we begin to obsess over the visible marker that the season is ready to turn with back-to-school sales and the return of morning traffic. This transition demands a rapid shift from the fluid flexibility of summer to the strictly choreographed schedule of fall, and several stakeholders pay the emotional and mental tax of pulling off the annual resurrection of structure.

Each stakeholder carries a weight

The process of going back to school is one that is discussed with joy and trepidation by both the student starting a new chapter and the parent finally getting back into routine. The reality, however, is that the success of back to school takes everyone, including teachers, coaches, guardians, and even the non-parental colleagues. It also doesn’t just start on the first day of school, but earlier, with countless decisions, tasks, and emotions that come before and after the first day.

Students, whether K-12 or college, have long worked to earn their grades, but their hardest work is internal during this transition. A child’s brain is adapting to social hierarchies and processing high levels of stimulation all while resisting the physical strain of sitting still for hours after months of unstructured movement. From small to large decisions, the weight compounds.

For teachers and coaches, the Review of Education notes that off-the-clock invisible labor is real and includes designing lesson plans, creating physical spaces to soothe sensory overload, or buying supplies with personal funds. Beyond logistics, the authors of Emotions in Education suggest that educators' primary invisible work involves emotional scaffolding as they prepare to absorb the anxieties of students' distinct personalities and work to build immediate trust with worried parents who have their own expectations.

For parents and guardians who could be called logistical micro-managers and may be experiencing decision fatigue, they are inundated tracking registration forms, following the appropriate apps, coordinating carpools, and marking calendars, all while also managing their day jobs. Emotionally they also bear a heavy duty absorbing their children’s stress while projecting a steadiness that they truly may not feel. Researchers in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships remind us how important it is for these actions to be acknowledged and handled appropriately because regulating one’s emotions superficially (surface acting) can be more harmful to the parents than genuine regulation (deep acting).

For organizations, 9-5 wasn’t designed for the school calendar, and progressive organizations have taken note by mitigating the invisible friction and enacting seasonal flexibility policies with core-hour meeting schedules (e.g., minimizing mandatory meetings prior to 10 a.m. or after 3 p.m.). Those that are not progressive enough to consider the ebbs and flows of the season have parents working in increased stress-induced environments and have the non-parent employees compensating for their colleagues. Building systemic buffers rather than expecting uninterrupted year-round output helps protect all employees (those who are parents and those who are not) from spillover work or burnout, boosts retention, and fosters an inclusive culture.

Why does the seasonal transition feel so draining?

The brain is an energy-conserving organ that relies heavily on patterns. So, when summer arrives, our routines disappear, forcing the brain into a state of continuous cognitive processing and possibly driving decision fatigue.

Structured routines lower cognitive load, stress, and anxiety by minimizing the number of decisions the brain makes each day. Also, consistent wake, sleep, and mealtimes regulate our internal body clock. And rhythms signal safety to the nervous systems, so to help everyone transition:

  • Establish anchors. Create stability with one or two daily non-negotiable anchors (e.g., a 10-minute walk, your morning journaling time, or a five-minute tea break).
  • Stage the night prior. Remove morning friction to conserve energy for the next day by preparing lunches, setting out clothes, and staging bags for school, work, or the gym.
  • Build in buffer time. Add an explicit 10-to-15-minute cushion to travel and/or transition schedules.
  • Implement a runway. Reserve the first 30 minutes after school or work for decompression to allow your nervous system to process the overstimulation before transitioning to the evening.

Long before the first bell or bus pick up, students, teachers, parents, and workplace colleagues are doing the heavy lifting that rarely shows up on the calendar, clock, or paycheck. As a starting point, we need to begin to see the work, acknowledge the work, and show appreciation for the invisible work that helps us all get to the things that are of importance to us.
